interactions.effect: Substantially reduced absorption of oral omadacycline (bioavailability markedly lowered), which can result in therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium chelate omadacycline in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing its absorption; the effect is pronounced enough that the label requires a fasting window.
interactions.management: Take oral omadacycline on an empty stomach, at least 4 hours before or after dairy products, antacids, or mineral supplements.
interactions.source: FDA Omadacycline Prescribing Information, Dosage and Administration / Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Reduced oral bioavailability of sarecycline, which can lower its effectiveness for acne treatment.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium form an insoluble chelate complex with sarecycline, reducing its gastrointestinal absorption.
interactions.management: Take sarecycline at least 2 hours before or after calcium-containing products, dairy, or other mineral supplements.
interactions.source: FDA Sarecycline Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Reduced oral bioavailability of the quinolone, which can result in therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium form an insoluble chelate complex with the quinolone, reducing its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
interactions.management: Take the quinolone at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing products, dairy, or other polyvalent-cation supplements.
interactions.source: Class effect of fluoroquinolones/quinolones; FDA Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Reduced oral bioavailability of the quinolone, which can result in therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium form an insoluble chelate complex with the quinolone, reducing its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
interactions.management: Take the quinolone at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing products, dairy, or other polyvalent-cation supplements.
interactions.source: Class effect of fluoroquinolones/quinolones; FDA Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Increased risk of CNS stimulation and convulsive seizures, particularly in patients with a seizure predisposition.
interactions.mechanism: Fluoroquinolones inhibit GABA-A receptors; NSAIDs are thought to add to this GABA-antagonist effect, increasing CNS excitability.
interactions.management: Use the combination with caution, especially in patients with a history of seizures or renal impairment; consider an alternative analgesic if there is a seizure risk factor.
interactions.source: Class effect of fluoroquinolone-NSAID interaction; FDA Lomefloxacin Prescribing Information, Warnings section

interactions.effect: Markedly increased theophylline plasma levels, with risk of theophylline toxicity (nausea, tachycardia, seizures); enoxacin produces the most pronounced effect of any quinolone on theophylline levels.
interactions.mechanism: Enoxacin is a potent inhibitor of CYP1A2, the principal enzyme responsible for theophylline metabolism.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination where possible; if unavoidable, reduce the theophylline dose substantially and monitor serum theophylline levels closely.
interactions.source: Classic, well-documented quinolone-theophylline interaction; FDA Enoxacin Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Reduced oral bioavailability of norfloxacin, which can result in therapeutic failure.
interactions.mechanism: Polyvalent cations such as calcium form an insoluble chelate complex with norfloxacin, reducing its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract.
interactions.management: Take norfloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing products, dairy, or other polyvalent-cation supplements.
interactions.source: FDA Norfloxacin Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Modestly increased theophylline plasma levels, with risk of theophylline toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Ofloxacin has a comparatively weak inhibitory effect on CYP1A2-mediated theophylline metabolism relative to enoxacin or ciprofloxacin, but the interaction is still documented.
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels if the combination is used, especially in patients already near the upper end of the therapeutic range.
interactions.source: FDA Ofloxacin Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Pefloxacin is a notable inhibitor of CYP1A2-mediated theophylline metabolism, second only to enoxacin among quinolones.
interactions.management: Reduce the theophylline dose and monitor serum levels closely if co-administration cannot be avoided.
interactions.source: Class effect of quinolone CYP1A2 inhibition; Drug Interaction Facts, quinolone monograph

interactions.effect: Markedly increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia (torsades de pointes) when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs.
interactions.mechanism: Sparfloxacin itself significantly prolongs the QT interval; combining it with other QT-prolonging agents such as pimozide has an additive effect on cardiac repolarization.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated; this marked QT liability was a major factor in sparfloxacin's restricted clinical use.
interactions.source: FDA Sparfloxacin Prescribing Information, Boxed Warning / Contraindications section

interactions.effect: Severe dysglycemia in both directions - hypoglycemia (potentiating glyburide) and, independently, hyperglycemia - a well-documented and clinically serious interaction.
interactions.mechanism: Gatifloxacin affects pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, altering insulin secretion; the resulting dysglycemic risk is amplified in patients on sulfonylureas.
interactions.management: Avoid gatifloxacin in patients on sulfonylureas where possible; if used, monitor blood glucose very closely, especially in elderly or diabetic patients.
interactions.source: This dysglycemia risk was a principal reason gatifloxacin (Tequin) was withdrawn from the US market; FDA Gatifloxacin Prescribing Information, Boxed Warning

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia; cardiotoxicity concerns led to grepafloxacin's withdrawal from the market.
interactions.mechanism: Grepafloxacin independently prolongs the QT interval; combining it with other QT-prolonging drugs such as pimozide has an additive effect.
interactions.management: Historical interaction of note only, since grepafloxacin was withdrawn from clinical use in 1999 due to cardiotoxicity, including reports associated with concomitant QT-prolonging drugs.
interactions.source: Grepafloxacin's cardiotoxicity-related withdrawal is well documented; FDA Grepafloxacin Prescribing Information (withdrawn)

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and torsades de pointes.
interactions.mechanism: Both moxifloxacin and pimozide independently prolong the QT interval; the effects are additive when combined.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated; use an alternative antibiotic in patients taking pimozide or other QT-prolonging drugs.
interactions.source: FDA Moxifloxacin Prescribing Information, Contraindications section

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and torsades de pointes.
interactions.mechanism: Both gemifloxacin and pimozide independently prolong the QT interval; the effects are additive when combined.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated; use an alternative antibiotic in patients taking pimozide or other QT-prolonging drugs.
interactions.source: FDA Gemifloxacin Prescribing Information, Contraindications section

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia (torsades de pointes), despite azithromycin's comparatively weak CYP3A4 inhibition.
interactions.mechanism: Azithromycin independently prolongs the QT interval to a modest degree; combined with pimozide's own marked QT effect, the risk becomes clinically significant even without a major pharmacokinetic boost in pimozide levels.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated; use an alternative antibiotic in patients taking pimozide.
interactions.source: FDA Azithromycin Prescribing Information, Warnings and Precautions (QT prolongation)

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of theophylline toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Roxithromycin is a moderate inhibitor of CYP3A4, reducing theophylline clearance, though less potently than erythromycin.
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels and reduce the dose if toxicity develops during roxithromycin therapy.
interactions.source: Roxithromycin Prescribing Information (ex-US); Drug Interaction Facts, macrolide monograph

interactions.effect: Theoretical additive QT-interval prolongation; dirithromycin's interaction potential is markedly lower than that of other macrolides.
interactions.mechanism: Dirithromycin is hydrolyzed non-enzymatically to its active form and does not significantly inhibit CYP3A4, unlike erythromycin or clarithromycin, but shares the macrolide class's mild QT-prolonging potential.
interactions.management: Standard macrolide QT caution applies, though clinically significant interaction is less likely than with erythromycin or clarithromycin.
interactions.source: FDA Dirithromycin Prescribing Information, Clinical Pharmacology section (minimal CYP450 interaction)

interactions.effect: Potential modest increase in fidaxomicin systemic absorption; clinically significant interaction is unlikely given fidaxomicin's minimal systemic absorption when used for C. difficile infection.
interactions.mechanism: Fidaxomicin and its active metabolite are substrates of the P-glycoprotein efflux transporter; potent P-glycoprotein inhibitors could theoretically increase systemic exposure.
interactions.management: No dose adjustment is generally required given fidaxomicin's local gut action, but be aware of the theoretical interaction with potent P-glycoprotein inhibitors.
interactions.source: FDA Fidaxomicin Prescribing Information, Clinical Pharmacology section (P-glycoprotein substrate)

interactions.effect: Theoretical additive QT-interval prolongation, extrapolated from the broader macrolide class.
interactions.mechanism: Macrolides can prolong the QT interval to varying degrees; specific human interaction data for this older or largely veterinary macrolide is limited, so the risk is extrapolated from better-studied class members.
interactions.management: Apply standard macrolide QT caution; specific dose guidance for this combination has not been well established in clinical studies.
interactions.source: Class-based extrapolation from macrolide QT-prolongation data; specific interaction studies for this agent are limited

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Josamycin is a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, reducing hepatic clearance of theophylline.
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels and reduce the dose if toxicity develops during josamycin therapy.
interactions.source: Josamycin Prescribing Information (ex-US, Japan/Europe); Drug Interaction Facts, macrolide monograph

interactions.effect: Increased carbamazepine plasma levels with risk of toxicity (ataxia, diplopia, confusion).
interactions.mechanism: Troleandomycin is one of the most potent CYP3A4 inhibitors among the macrolides, historically exploited clinically to boost corticosteroid levels in severe asthma.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination where possible; monitor carbamazepine levels closely if troleandomycin cannot be avoided.
interactions.source: Troleandomycin's potent CYP3A4-inhibiting property is well documented from its historical use as a steroid-sparing agent; Drug Interaction Facts, macrolide monograph

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of toxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Midecamycin, like other 16-membered macrolides, has moderate CYP3A4-inhibiting activity, reducing theophylline clearance.
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels and reduce the dose if toxicity develops during midecamycin therapy.
interactions.source: Class-based extrapolation from 16-membered macrolide CYP3A4 inhibition; specific interaction studies for midecamycin are limited

interactions.effect: Increased risk of QT-interval prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
interactions.mechanism: Telithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor and independently prolongs the QT interval; combined with pimozide's own QT effect, the risk is additive and significant.
interactions.management: Concurrent use is contraindicated.
interactions.source: FDA Telithromycin Prescribing Information, Boxed Warning / Contraindications section

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of toxicity, extrapolated from cethromycin's ketolide structure shared with telithromycin.
interactions.mechanism: Cethromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor by virtue of its ketolide structure, similar to telithromycin, though clinical interaction data are more limited since cethromycin was never fully approved in the US.
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels if co-administered; specific dose-adjustment data are limited.
interactions.source: Extrapolated from ketolide-class CYP3A4 inhibition; cethromycin clinical trial data (not FDA-approved)

interactions.effect: Increased theophylline plasma levels with risk of toxicity, extrapolated from solithromycin's ketolide/macrolide CYP3A4-inhibiting structure.
interactions.mechanism: Solithromycin, like other ketolides, inhibits CYP3A4, reducing theophylline clearance; clinical interaction data are limited as the drug was not granted FDA approval (hepatotoxicity signal in trials).
interactions.management: Monitor serum theophylline levels if co-administered; specific dose-adjustment data are limited since solithromycin has not reached routine clinical use.
interactions.source: Extrapolated from ketolide-class CYP3A4 inhibition; solithromycin clinical trial data (not FDA-approved)

interactions.effect: Markedly elevated everolimus blood concentrations, with increased risk of everolimus toxicity (stomatitis, myelosuppression, pneumonitis, nephrotoxicity).
interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin is a moderate-to-strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; everolimus is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4 and is also a P-glycoprotein substrate.
interactions.management: Avoid concurrent use where possible; if required, reduce the everolimus dose substantially and monitor trough levels closely.
interactions.source: FDA Everolimus Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section (moderate/strong CYP3A4 inhibitors)

interactions.effect: Increased pimecrolimus blood concentration with topical use, particularly over large or broken skin areas.
interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, which metabolizes pimecrolimus; although pimecrolimus is applied topically, systemic absorption can be clinically relevant when used on extensive or compromised skin.
interactions.management: Use with caution in patients on strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, especially when pimecrolimus is applied over large body surface areas.
interactions.source: FDA Pimecrolimus (Elidel) Prescribing Information, Drug Interactions section

interactions.effect: Additive ototoxicity (potentially irreversible hearing loss and vestibular damage) and nephrotoxicity.
interactions.mechanism: Both drugs are independently oto- and nephrotoxic; furosemide-induced volume depletion can also raise aminoglycoside concentrations in renal and cochlear tissue.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination where possible; if it cannot be avoided, use the lowest effective furosemide dose, dose the aminoglycoside by weight and renal function, and monitor renal function and hearing (audiometry) closely.
interactions.source: Class effect of aminoglycoside-loop diuretic ototoxicity; Lawson DH et al., "Effect of furosemide on the pharmacokinetics of gentamicin in patients", J Clin Pharmacol 1982

interactions.effect: Carbapenems can cut serum valproic acid concentrations by roughly 60–100% within about 24 hours, often causing breakthrough seizures. This is a class effect seen with every carbapenem.
interactions.mechanism: Not fully settled. Proposed: carbapenems inhibit acylpeptide hydrolase, which normally converts valproate glucuronide back to active valproate, so valproate is cleared faster; reduced enterohepatic recycling and altered red-cell distribution may add to it.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination. Choose a non-carbapenem antibiotic where possible. If a carbapenem is essential, add another antiseizure medicine (for example levetiracetam or a benzodiazepine) — raising the valproate dose does not usually overcome the drop. Levels can stay low for 1–2 weeks after the carbapenem is stopped, so monitor for seizures and recheck levels.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Primaxin (imipenem-cilastatin)); Mancl EE, Gidal BE. The effect of carbapenem antibiotics on plasma concentrations of valproic acid. Ann Pharmacother 2009;43(12):2082-7

interactions.mechanism: Not fully settled. Proposed: carbapenems inhibit acylpeptide hydrolase, which normally converts valproate glucuronide back to active valproate, so valproate is cleared faster; reduced enterohepatic recycling and altered red-cell distribution may add to it.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination. Choose a non-carbapenem antibiotic where possible. If a carbapenem is essential, add another antiseizure medicine (for example levetiracetam or a benzodiazepine) — raising the valproate dose does not usually overcome the drop. Levels can stay low for 1–2 weeks after the carbapenem is stopped, so monitor for seizures and recheck levels.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Doribax (doripenem)); Mancl EE, Gidal BE. The effect of carbapenem antibiotics on plasma concentrations of valproic acid. Ann Pharmacother 2009;43(12):2082-7

interactions.effect: Generalized seizures have been reported in patients receiving ganciclovir together with imipenem-cilastatin.
interactions.mechanism: Not well defined; imipenem lowers the seizure threshold (GABA-A antagonism) and ganciclovir has CNS toxicity, so additive excitability is likely.
interactions.management: Avoid unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk; use another antibiotic where possible. If used together, watch for CNS effects and adjust both drugs for renal function.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Primaxin (imipenem-cilastatin); ganciclovir/valganciclovir)

interactions.effect: Risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, clonus) when linezolid is combined with a serotonergic drug.
interactions.mechanism: Linezolid is a weak reversible non-selective MAO inhibitor, so serotonin builds up when a serotonergic agent is added.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination if possible. If linezolid is essential, stop or substitute the serotonergic drug and monitor closely for 2 weeks (5 weeks for fluoxetine) or until 24 h after the last linezolid dose.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Zyvox linezolid)

interactions.effect: Risk of serotonin syndrome when linezolid is combined with an SSRI.
interactions.mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect from MAO inhibition plus serotonin reuptake blockade.
interactions.management: Avoid where possible; if unavoidable, monitor closely for serotonin syndrome and consider withholding the SSRI (fluoxetine has a long half-life).
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Zyvox linezolid)

interactions.effect: Additive risk of nephrotoxicity (and ototoxicity) when vancomycin is combined with an aminoglycoside.
interactions.mechanism: Both drugs injure proximal tubular cells and the inner ear; the effects add together.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination if possible; if used, monitor renal function and drug levels closely and keep the courses as short as possible.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (vancomycin, gentamicin)

interactions.effect: Additive risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity when teicoplanin is combined with an aminoglycoside.
interactions.mechanism: Overlapping renal and cochlear toxicity.
interactions.management: Monitor renal function and hearing; avoid where possible.
interactions.source: Teicoplanin (Targocid) summary of product characteristics (EMC)

interactions.effect: Combining colistin with an aminoglycoside markedly increases the risk of nephrotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade.
interactions.mechanism: Both drugs are nephrotoxic and have neuromuscular-blocking activity; the effects are additive.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination unless there is no alternative; monitor renal function daily and watch for weakness or breathing difficulty.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Coly-Mycin M colistimethate)

interactions.effect: Concurrent aminoglycosides increase the risk of nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade with polymyxin B.
interactions.mechanism: Additive kidney and nerve toxicity; both can cause neuromuscular blockade.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination where possible; if unavoidable, monitor renal function and watch for respiratory depression.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (polymyxin B for injection, boxed warning)

interactions.effect: Concurrent aminoglycosides increase the risk of nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity and neuromuscular blockade with polymyxin B.

interactions.effect: Concurrent sulfonamides with methenamine can form an insoluble precipitate in urine, causing crystalluria.
interactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde released from methenamine in acid urine reacts with sulfonamides to form insoluble complexes.
interactions.management: Avoid the combination (contraindicated in the methenamine label).
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Hiprex methenamine hippurate)

interactions.effect: Metronidazole can raise phenytoin concentrations and cause phenytoin toxicity (ataxia, nystagmus).
interactions.mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits the hepatic metabolism of phenytoin (CYP2C9).
interactions.management: Monitor phenytoin levels and clinical signs when starting or stopping metronidazole; adjust the phenytoin dose if needed.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Flagyl metronidazole)

interactions.effect: In vitro antagonism: erythromycin can reduce clindamycin’s effect by blocking its ribosomal binding site and inducing resistance.
interactions.mechanism: Both drugs bind overlapping sites on the 50S ribosomal subunit; macrolides can also induce MLSB resistance.
interactions.management: Avoid using these two together; choose one agent unless the combination is specifically advised.
interactions.source: FDA/DailyMed prescribing information (Cleocin clindamycin)
